title: Common Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
summary: The recurring, avoidable mistakes — cutting across any single phase of the round — that sink otherwise technically strong candidates.

slides.markdown:
Most failed coding rounds aren't failed on algorithm knowledge — they're failed on a short, recurring list of behavioral mistakes that have nothing to do with whether you knew the right technique. A candidate who knows sliding windows cold can still fail by coding silently, ignoring a hint, or losing track of the clock.

This topic is a cross-cutting checklist: coding before stating an approach, ignoring interviewer signals, illegible code, losing time across multiple problems, and over-engineering a simple ask. Treat it as a pre-round self-check, not a first-time read.

The single most common way a technically correct solution scores lower than it should: typing the first idea that comes to mind instead of stating it first and getting a nod. This matters for two reasons. First, communication is graded on its own axis — a silent typist gives the interviewer nothing to evaluate until code appears, and by then a wrong turn is expensive to unwind. Second, stating the approach first is cheap insurance: if it's the wrong approach, the interviewer can redirect you in ten seconds instead of after five minutes of typed code.

The fix is mechanical: after reading the prompt and clarifying constraints, say the approach in one or two sentences — "I'll use a hash map to track counts, then a single pass to find the answer" — and only start typing once you've said it.

When an interviewer says "are you sure that handles duplicates?" or offers a nudge toward a different data structure, it is almost never idle conversation — it's usually a deliberate signal that something is off, delivered gently so you can catch it yourself. Continuing to code past it, or acknowledging it verbally but not actually changing course, reads as either not having heard the signal or not knowing how to act on it — both worse than the original issue the hint was pointing at.

Treat any pushback as data worth pausing for: stop, restate what they said in your own words, and explicitly decide whether it changes your approach before continuing. Even if you conclude the original approach is fine, saying why out loud is far better than silently ignoring the question.

Single-letter names beyond a loop index (`a`, `b`, `x1`), no whitespace or function boundaries, and dense one-liners that pack three operations into a single line all make your code harder for the interviewer to follow live — and code quality is graded as its own rubric line, not folded silently into "did it work."

This doesn't mean over-engineering structure into a 20-line problem (see the over-engineering pitfall below) — it means basic hygiene costs nothing under time pressure and pays for itself immediately: name variables for what they hold (`left`, `right`, `seen` instead of `l`, `r`, `s`), break a dense expression into two named steps if a reader would have to pause on it, and use a small helper function when a piece of logic is reused rather than duplicating it inline.

slides.sectionTitle: Losing track of time across a multi-problem round
slides.markdown:
A 45-minute round with two problems doesn't mean 22.5 minutes each — the first problem is usually meant to be finished in 15-20 minutes so there's real time left for a second, harder one. A candidate who spends 35 minutes perfecting the first problem's edge cases can run out the clock before attempting the second at all, which usually costs more than a slightly rougher first solution would have.

The practical habit: check in on time explicitly, out loud, at natural checkpoints — after stating your approach, and again once the first version compiles. "I'm about 20 minutes in and have a working solution — let me do a quick pass on edge cases and then we can move to the next one" shows time-awareness the interviewer would otherwise have to manage for you.

Building an abstract `Strategy` interface, a config object, and three helper classes for a problem that's genuinely solved by a fifteen-line loop is a real, common failure — not a display of skill. It burns time that should go to correctness and testing, and it often signals the opposite of seniority: senior engineers are known for matching solution complexity to problem complexity, not defaulting to maximum structure regardless of scale.

The practical check: before adding an abstraction, ask whether the problem as stated actually needs it, or whether you're adding it out of habit. A direct, well-named, well-tested fifteen-line function usually scores higher than a twelve-file "enterprise" version of the same logic — and it leaves you far more of the clock to actually finish and test.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: strong vs weak candidates in the first two minutes
slides.markdown:
Interviewers report forming an early read within the first two minutes of a problem, often before any code is written, based on behavior that has nothing to do with algorithm knowledge yet.

| | Weak first two minutes | Strong first two minutes |
|---|---|---|
| On reading the prompt | Starts typing immediately | Reads aloud, restates the problem in own words |
| On ambiguity | Assumes and proceeds silently | Asks 1-2 targeted clarifying questions |
| On approach | Jumps to code with no stated plan | States approach and expected complexity first |
| On constraints | Ignores stated input size / bounds | Uses bounds to sanity-check approach ("n up to 10^5 rules out O(n²)") |

None of this requires knowing the answer yet — it's entirely about process, which is exactly why it's gradable before a single line of code exists.

slides.sectionTitle: Why technically strong candidates still fail on these
slides.markdown:
These pitfalls are dangerous specifically because they're orthogonal to algorithm knowledge — a candidate can know exactly the right technique and still fail by triggering three of these in the same round. Interview scoring is typically multi-axis (correctness, communication, complexity, code quality), and a strong score on one axis doesn't offset a weak score on another the way a single overall "smart enough" impression might in an unstructured conversation.

The senior-level nuance: these pitfalls compound under stress, not independently. Someone who freezes briefly (see `handling-being-stuck`) is more likely to then skip stating an approach when they resume, which is more likely to lead to silently ignoring a hint because narration has already stopped. Catching the first slip early prevents the chain.

A short list to run through, silently, right before a round starts: Am I going to state my approach before typing? Am I going to actually act on pushback, not just acknowledge it? Are my variable names going to be readable to someone seeing this code for the first time? Do I have a rough time budget for each problem, and will I check in on it out loud? Is my planned solution's complexity matched to what the problem actually needs?

Running this checklist takes under a minute and catches the pitfalls that have nothing to do with algorithm prep — the kind that no amount of additional LeetCode practice fixes, because they're behavioral habits, not knowledge gaps.

In post-round debriefs, interviewers rarely cite a single isolated mistake — they more often describe a pattern across the round: the candidate coded silently *and* lost track of time *and* didn't react when nudged. Any one of these alone is recoverable; two or three together read as a genuine pattern rather than a one-off slip, which is what actually drives a no-hire decision on an otherwise-correct solution.

This is why the self-check above is worth running as a whole list rather than fixing whichever single pitfall you personally struggled with last time — the risk isn't any one item, it's the compounding.

Several of these pitfalls have their own dedicated topics with more depth: silent coding is covered fully in [narrating your approach](narrating-your-approach), and freezing or apologizing under pressure in [handling being stuck](handling-being-stuck). For the complexity-matching half of the over-engineering pitfall, see [talking through complexity](complexity-communication).
